newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN considers approving Central Africa peacekeepers.
newsitem.headline: UN considers approving Central Africa peacekeepers.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council is considering authorising an inter-African monitoring force in the Central African Republic that has been operating without international approval, diplomats said on Wednesday.

Council endorsement would not entail putting the force of about 700, organised after army rebellions, under a U.N. peacekeeping umbrella and thereby having it financed by all members. Instead it would approve the contingent, as the Council did for Albania, and give it some parameters and international respectability.

Some members, particularly the United States, are hesitating because it would mean endorsing a force retroactively but most Western diplomats say it would set conditions and give its mandate more clarity.
The formal request originally came on July 4 from Ange-Felix Patasse, president of the Central African Republic.
It is being pushed in the council by France, which plans to pull its 1,400 troops out of the Central African Republic and perhaps keep 100 soldiers at the airport.

French troops have intervened several times to protect the government from army mutinies over pay and other complaints. But the new French government now is reviewing its military and political role in its former African colonies.

Separately, the inter-African mission was set up earlier this year and includes soldiers from Bukina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal and Togo. They were to disarm rebels and help maintain security after mutinies that turned into a campaign to oust Patasse, a civilian elected in 1993.
Patasse, in his letter, released on Wednesday, said the Africa force was to disarm the former rebels and militia supporting the army rebellions that first broke out in 1996.
He said the mission wanted authorisation for the use of force to defend itself following June attacks against them.

Mali's respected former military leader, Amadou Toumani Toure, brokered a January deal to end the mutinies. He moved in to re-estabish the peace accords after weeklong clashes broke out again in June between army dissidents and the African peacekeepers.
